title: Mirror Phrase Contest
story: A word-puzzle club runs a contest for phrases that read the same forwards and backwards, like "Top spot." or "12:21". The judges look only at letters and digits, ignoring spaces and punctuation, and capitals count the same as small letters.
So "Top spot." is judged as topspot, which mirrors perfectly. With thousands of entries, the club wants a program for the first round.
task: Write isMirrorPhrase(entry). Return true if the letters and digits of entry read the same left to right as right to left, ignoring case. Otherwise return false.
Every character that is not a letter (a-z, A-Z) or digit (0-9) is ignored. Digits must mirror like letters. An entry with no letters or digits counts as a mirror phrase.
constraints: entry contains printable ASCII characters only (letters, digits, spaces, punctuation).

examples.explanation: Letters and digits, lowercased: topspot. Backwards it is still topspot, so it passes.
The letters are steponpets; backwards, stepnopets. The ends match (s and s, t and t, e and e, p and p) until o meets n, so it fails.
Digits count. The characters are 0 and p, which differ. Throwing digits away would leave just p and wrongly answer true.

hints: Take "Top spot.". Which character must the first T match, where is it, and what did you skip to reach it?
Check from both ends at once: the first counted character against the last, the second against the second last, and so on.
Put one finger at the start and one at the end. If a finger is on a space or mark, move just that finger inward and look again.

Use left and right indexes. Skip characters that are not letters or digits. When both point at real characters, compare them in lowercase: if they differ, return false; if they match, move both inward. Stop when they meet.
bruteForce: Build a cleaned lowercase copy of just the letters and digits, reverse it, and compare.
That is correct and O(n), fine at this size, but it builds two extra strings as long as the input. Checking from both ends of the original needs no copies and stops at the first mismatch.

walkthrough: A mirror phrase pairs its first counted character with its last, its second with its second last, and so on. So check those pairs directly from both ends of the original string, skipping anything that does not count.
• left = 0 (T), right = 8 (.). The period does not count. Move right to 7.
• left is on the space. Skip it: left = 4 = right, so the loop ends. Every pair matched: return true.
The middle character needs no partner, so the loop stops when the indexes meet.
solution.timeWhy: Every step moves one or both indexes inward, so the loop runs at most n times.
solution.spaceWhy: The algorithm keeps two indexes and builds no cleaned or reversed copy.
solution.takeaway: To check a symmetric property, walk inward from both ends and compare pairs. To ignore some items, let each pointer skip them on its own side instead of building a filtered copy.
